a16z just published “You Need a New CFO”, and it’s worth a read: https://lnkd.in/duxnBgtf ☀️ The short version: finance is no longer defined by who can report the numbers or raise the capital. The scarce skill is designing the operating system the company runs on, now that software does a growing part of the work itself.

That doesn’t only change the CFO seat. Accounting moves from reconciling to setting the rules, owning the controls and signing off. FP&A moves from annual budgets to continuous decisions. Smaller teams, more leverage, more senior judgment.

Most companies will get there by retrofitting. At ALVA Energie, we want to design it from day one. And we’re doing it on a business that isn’t easy to model. We install, own and operate solar assets on residential and commercial buildings, and we supply the energy. Physical assets, many entities, long-lived contracts, financing and operations all at once.

There’s no off-the-shelf playbook for this. Someone has to build the operating model.

I’m looking for the spearhead of FP&A who has spent time in the machine room: someone who can trace a number back to its driver, who gets uncomfortable when the model “roughly works”, and who then turns around and asks what the business could become if we scaled this 10x. Detail orientation and a growth mindset in the same person. AI and automation are the tools that let one person carry that scope. They don’t replace the thinking.

You’d build the planning and operating model from a clean sheet, with a direct line to the CFO and real influence on how ALVA allocates capital.
It sits right next to the Group Accounting build we started earlier. Accounting creates the foundation of truth. FP&AI turns it into foresight.

A six-month contract can change your career. It can also leave you paying for a move long after the job ends. 💸

That’s the part of contract relocation people underestimate.

The recruiter sees a start date. 📅

You see the opportunity.

But somewhere between the offer and the first day, real obligations start stacking up:

1) Temporary housing
2) Security deposits
3) Travel and moving costs
4) A lease that may outlive the assignment
5) Possibly two homes at the same time
6) And a contract that could end earlier than expected

For full-time employees, relocation support may be built into the offer.

For contractors, the contract itself often becomes the safety net. 🛡️

That means the questions you ask before signing matter enormously.

- What happens if the project ends early?
- Who covers the trip home?
- When is the stipend actually paid?
- Is there a minimum guaranteed term?
- Can housing commitments be unwound quickly?
- And does the rate still make sense after the true cost of relocating is calculated?

A big hourly rate can look extraordinary on paper. 💰

Then housing, travel, insurance, duplicate living expenses and taxes enter the picture.

Suddenly, the number that matters isn’t the rate.

It’s what remains. 💡

If you’re considering relocating for a contract role or hiring professionals who are, this Relo.AI guide breaks down the costs, contract protections, housing decisions and questions worth examining before the move.

January 1, 2027 is less than three months away. 

The biggest employment changes are state laws, and most land that day.

What I would put on the 2027 list:AI in people decisions. 

Colorado’s rewritten AI law adds notice, human review, and recordkeeping duties, and it reaches applicants and employees even if your company sits in another state. 
California bars relying solely on an automated system to discipline or fire someone, starting July 1.

Layoffs tied to automation. From January 1, California WARN notices must add detail when AI or automation drove the layoff.

Stay-or-pay agreements. California applies its limits to contracts signed on or after January 1. New York’s Trapped at Work Act follows on February 13 for employers of any size.

Paid leave. Connecticut paid sick leave covers employers with a single employee. Illinois requires regular pay for jury duty at employers with over 25 people.

Pay floors. California’s exempt salary minimum becomes $72,384. New York’s minimum wage holds on January 1, at $17 in New York City, Long Island, and Westchester and $16 elsewhere.

Most of this reaches HR before it reaches legal. If you operate in several states, one handbook doesn't work.

Start with an inventory of where AI touches hiring, discipline, and exits. Finish it before December.

Every few years, someone declares the end of Indian IT. The latest round came in February, when the Nifty IT index had its worst day since March 2020.

Rahul Jindal & I spent the last few days working through this question & debating various aspects, and I’m glad to share what we wrote: “Indian IT’s sixth reinvention.”

Between the two of us, we see what these tools can do, what they can’t do alone, and we’ve heard this call before. Y2K, the dot-com bust, 2008, the 2016 automation scare and COVID were each supposed to be the end. Each time, the industry came back larger.

Most of the commentary frames this as the industry versus AI. We think that’s the wrong frame. The engineers, architects and delivery leads at these firms are among the heaviest users of these tools. The real question is what them plus AI looks like.

Here is where we landed:
1. The industry comes through, but the pyramid doesn’t. In our base case, revenue at the majors is up about 10% by FY32 while headcount is down about 15%. In all five earlier shocks, headcount survived. This time even our optimistic case has it shrinking.
2. The product shifts from hours to accountability. Outcome pricing has arrived in business services. Nobody has yet taken real liability for agent failures. Our prediction, which you can hold us to: by the end of 2028, an Indian major signs an insured, liability-bearing agent contract.
3. Clients capture most of the gains. They buy roughly 70% more work for about 10% more money. Model providers take a new slice. Shareholders get a little. The people who stay get paid more, but there are fewer of them.
4. The whole case rests on one number: whether clients buy more work as its price falls. If they don’t, our base case becomes the bear case. We put odds on all three scenarios and show the math.
5. The most urgent risk is the talent pipeline. Indian IT’s real training system was the job itself. If firms stop hiring juniors because AI can do their work today, they stop building tomorrow’s seniors. Without more investment in skilling and education, we think the curve could bend down sharply from around 2032.

We also lay out eight signposts we’ll track every quarter, so you can tell if we’re wrong. If they go the wrong way, we’ll say so.

One thing I’d stress: the numbers are our estimates, built to be argued with. If you work in IT services, in a GCC, in an AI-native startup, or on the client side, I’d genuinely like to hear where you disagree.

The full paper is attached as a document. It’s a 15-minute read.

Thank you, Rahul Jindal, for being the best kind of co-author: someone who pushes back until the argument gets better.

Even with unlimited budget, the legal leaders around the table still wanted more people (not tech).

That was my biggest takeaway from last week’s Our Legal Community Leadership Table, hosted by Anne Graue in partnership with Ivo.

Following a fireside discussion on AI with James Hooper and Umran Kadir, we were asked how we’d spend an unlimited budget. Despite AI being the key topic of the evening, many answers were actually people-related: hiring more lawyers, bringing in a legal technologist or better rewarding the team already doing the work.

Those answers reflected something familiar to anyone running a lean legal team. There is plenty of ambition to improve how things work, alongside a full inbox of contracts, negotiations and questions that need attention today.

Turning that ambition into progress takes people with the time and expertise to carry it through. A legal technologist can help a team select and get more from its tools. An experienced lawyer can take ownership of the day-to-day work that would otherwise keep the GC tied up.

Both create capacity to move forward. And for teams whose workload is growing, deciding where that capacity is needed is an important starting point.

At Size Seven, we provide experienced fractional legal support shaped around those pressures. If your legal team needs more capacity to move things forward, get in touch.

Thank you to Anne and Ivo for a thought-provoking evening. Great to catch up Alexandra Geelan and meet Sian Story too.

A year ago, I was a VC at Insight Partners by day, tinkering on Tenix Health by night. Today, we’re announcing our $4M+ seed round, led by Insight co-founder Jeff Horing and joined by Refract Ventures 🎉

We’re starting by addressing a deceptively simple question that’s surprisingly hard for providers to answer: “are we getting paid what we’re owed by insurance?”

Imagine you’re a revenue cycle analyst: you submit a claim to insurance, billing $100. Your contract says you should be paid $90. Weeks later, you get a remittance that pays $80, with the $10 contract underpayment hidden as a routine adjustment.

You can’t catch an underpayment if you don’t know what you were owed. Calculating that number requires tediously loading contract rates into a fee schedule, applying variable terms for each encounter, and checking the result against every remittance. With a backlog of unpaid claims, that work usually doesn’t happen.

We built Tenix Health so providers can stop writing off earned revenue. Our AI Revenue Cycle Analyst structures contracts and billing data, finds the leakage, works the appeal, and reports on what it recovered.

“The AI did it” is not an accountability plan.

When an AI system makes a harmful mistake, who is responsible—the developer, the vendor, the organization using it or the person relying on its output?

There is no universal answer. Legal liability depends on the facts, applicable law, contracts and each party’s conduct.

But leaders should not wait for a lawsuit to ask the question.

Before deploying AI, an organization should be able to answer:

• Who approves its use, and for which tasks?
• What decisions require human review?
• Who checks accuracy and monitors failures?
• What do the vendor contract and insurance actually cover?
• Who can stop the system, correct an error and help someone harmed by it?

A human “in the loop” means little if that person lacks the time, training or authority to challenge the output.

The stakes are especially high when AI influences healthcare, hiring, public benefits or public safety. People need a meaningful way to question a decision and reach someone empowered to fix it.

AI can support decisions. It should not become a way to avoid responsibility for them.

The responsible approach is to define accountability before deployment—not negotiate it after someone gets hurt.
